reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Gastric outlet obstruction is a mechanical or functional blockage of gastric emptying at the antrum, pylorus or proximal duodenum, presenting with postprandial vomiting of undigested food, early satiety, bloating and weight loss.
In adults, malignancy (pancreatic, gastric antral or duodenal carcinoma) has overtaken peptic ulcer disease as the leading cause, so any new obstruction warrants exclusion of cancer.
Chronic vomiting of gastric contents produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria, a classic and important electrolyte disturbance to recognise and correct.
A succussion splash heard several hours after a meal and a visibly distended stomach are useful bedside signs of retained gastric content.
Initial management is nasogastric decompression, correction of dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities, and acid suppression before definitive treatment.
Endoscopy with biopsy is central to establishing benign versus malignant aetiology, and cross-sectional imaging defines the extent of any tumour.
Benign strictures may respond to endoscopic balloon dilatation, while malignant obstruction is palliated by enteral stenting or surgical gastrojejunostomy depending on prognosis and fitness.
In infants, hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is the classic cause, presenting with non-bilious projectile vomiting and a palpable pyloric olive, and is a distinct paediatric entity.
reference.pathophysiology: Gastric outlet obstruction results from any process that mechanically narrows or functionally impairs the antropyloric or proximal duodenal outflow tract. Benign mechanical causes include peptic ulcer disease, where acute pyloric channel oedema or chronic fibrotic scarring narrows the lumen, as well as caustic-injury strictures, Crohn disease and rarely bezoars or prolapsing polyps. Malignant causes include distal gastric adenocarcinoma, periampullary and pancreatic head tumours invading or compressing the duodenum, and duodenal tumours. Obstruction leads to retention of ingested food and gastric secretions, progressive gastric dilatation and eventually mucosal ischaemia and atony. Persistent vomiting of hydrochloric-acid-rich gastric fluid produces loss of chloride and hydrogen ions with a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; secondary hypokalaemia and volume depletion drive renal potassium and hydrogen excretion, causing the characteristic paradoxical aciduria. Chronic obstruction also impairs nutrition and causes weight loss.
additionalDifferentials: gastroparesis and other functional gastric motility disorders
peptic ulcer disease with pyloric channel scarring
bezoar, caustic stricture or annular pancreas
additionalInvestigations: upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy of any stricture or mass
serum electrolytes, renal function and blood gas to characterise metabolic alkalosis
contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen to stage malignancy and define anatomy
upper gastrointestinal contrast study to demonstrate the level of obstruction
gastric emptying study when a functional disorder such as gastroparesis is suspected
full blood count and nutritional assessment including albumin
redFlags: signs of perforation with peritonism and sepsis
severe dehydration with metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia
weight loss, anorexia or a palpable epigastric mass suggesting malignancy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on aetiology: benign obstruction from peptic disease or a dilatable stricture generally has a good outcome once corrected, whereas malignant obstruction carries the prognosis of the underlying cancer and is often managed palliatively. Prompt correction of fluid and electrolyte derangement is essential to reduce perioperative risk.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise and correct hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis before intervention.
Assuming a benign peptic cause and not biopsying to exclude malignancy.
Confusing functional gastroparesis with true mechanical obstruction.
Inadequate gastric decompression leading to aspiration.
Overlooking nutritional depletion that needs correction before definitive treatment.

Give acid suppression with a proton-pump inhibitor, particularly for peptic aetiology
Establish the aetiology with endoscopy and biopsy of any stricture or mass, distinguishing benign from malignant disease
For benign peptic strictures, undertake endoscopic balloon dilatation together with proton-pump inhibition and Helicobacter pylori eradication
For malignant obstruction, offer surgical resection or gastrojejunostomy, or endoscopic self-expanding metal stenting for palliation
Provide nutritional support and correct deficiencies before definitive treatment
Manage through gastroenterology, surgery and oncology as dictated by the cause
